land.text: the principality between the Danube and the Stara Planina range, including Sofia, created by the Treaty of Berlin (13 July 1878)

predecessors.note: Bulgaria remained an Ottoman vassal in law ('a legal fiction' per the Principality page) until the declaration of independence of 5 October 1908.

land.text: Bulgaria within its post-1940 borders (Southern Dobruja kept, Greek and Yugoslav lands renounced) when 'Monarchy abolished: 15 September 1946'

successors.note: The monarchy was abolished on 15 September 1946 (Kingdom of Bulgaria page). Cliopatria has no Bulgarian row for 1945-1946, carries the state as a single 'Kingdom of Bulgaria' shape in 1947 (Q147909, 110,018 km2) and as the People's Republic from 1948 (Q121932); this dossier ends at the abolition, the republican row should start there.

capitals.name: Sofia
capitals.note: Principality page infobox: 'Sofia (1878-1908)'; Kingdom page: 'Capital: Sofia'. The infobox also lists Plovdiv (1878, the Eastern Rumelian capital) and Tarnovo (1879, where the Constituent Assembly met and the constitution was adopted on 28 April 1879); neither was the seat of the principality's government.

rulers.name: Provisional Russian Administration in Bulgaria
rulers.title: Russian provisional administration
rulers.note: Principality page infobox: capital 'Sofia (1878-1908)' with the note '(Provisional Russian Administration in Bulgaria)' and 'until June 1879'; Alexander of Battenberg is listed from 29 April 1879, so the two overlap in 1879.

rulers.name: Alexander I (Alexander of Battenberg)
rulers.title: Prince
rulers.note: 29 April 1879 to 7 September 1886, abdicated (Principality page); the 1886-1887 interval is the regency below.

rulers.name: Regency (Stefan Stambolov, Sava Mutkurov, Petko Karavelov)
rulers.title: Regents
rulers.note: Principality page infobox lists the three as rulers for 1886-1887, after Alexander's abdication; Ferdinand is listed from 29 April 1887 in the table, although the body says he was elected in July 1887.

rulers.name: Ferdinand I
rulers.title: Prince, from 5 October 1908 Tsar
rulers.note: 29 April 1887 to 5 October 1908 as prince (Principality page); 'Ferdinand I: 1908-1918' as tsar (Kingdom page).

rulers.name: Boris III
rulers.title: Tsar
rulers.note: 1918-1943, died August 1943; 'Authoritarian absolute monarchy (1935-1943) (de facto)' after his April 1935 counter-coup.

rulers.name: Simeon II
rulers.title: Tsar (child, under a regency)
rulers.note: Regency headed by Prince Kiril with Bogdan Filov and Nikola Mihov; monarchy abolished 15 September 1946.

correction.text: the principality 'between the Danube and the Stara Planina range, including Sofia' that the Treaty of Berlin of 13 July 1878 created; Eastern Rumelia, south of the range, is a separate autonomous Ottoman province and Macedonia is returned to the Sultan

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria's first Bulgarian shape begins in 1880 but the page says the principality 'was established by the Treaty of Berlin in 1878' (infobox 13 July 1878); Alexander of Battenberg reigns from 29 April 1879. The page dates no border change between 1878 and 1880, so the 1880 outline is used. The page gives no area.

63,416 km2 for 1880-1884; the Principality page gives no area, so no infobox comparison is possible. The outline fits the Berlin settlement as the page words it (north of Stara Planina and the Sofia region, Eastern Rumelia excluded): the 1885 shape has 130 more gazetteer cells, all between 41.3 and 42.9 N.

99,673 km2 for 1885-1911. Adds Eastern Rumelia (the gazetteer difference to the 1880 shape is about 32,900 km2, bbox 24.2-27.7 E, 41.3-42.9 N), which the unification page places between the Balkan Mountains and the Rila and Rhodope Mountains; coup at Plovdiv on 18 September [6 September O.S.] 1885, de jure recognition by the Tophane Agreement of 5 April 1886. The page gives no area. The shape runs through 1908 unchanged: independence on 5 October 1908 is a rename, not a border change.

correction.text: Cliopatria's 1912 outline without Adrianople; every other land won since October 1912 in Thrace and Eastern Macedonia is contested with the Ottoman Empire until the Treaty of London (30 May 1913), because that treaty 'ceded' the Ottoman land west of the Enos-Midiya line to the Balkan League and left its division among the allies 'undecided'

keyframe_review.note: 153,443 km2: the shape draws every conquest of the First Balkan War as Bulgarian from 1912, including Edirne (the gazetteer finds it in the shape) which the page says Bulgarian forces conquered only after the failed Ottoman counterattack of January 1913. The ledger carries the conquest zone (1912 shape minus 1885 shape, about 47,800 km2) as contested from October 1912 and as gained, in part, in 1913. The Kingdom page gives 122,134 km2 for 1915, not 1912; no infobox figure for 1912.

111,800 km2 for 1913-1915 against 122,134 km2 (Kingdom of Bulgaria infobox, 1915; ratio 0.92) and 114,424 km2 (Bulgaria during World War I page, about September 1915; ratio 0.98). The outline matches the Treaty of Bucharest (10 August 1913) as the page words it: 'a portion of Macedonia, including the town of Strumnitza' and 'western Thrace with a 70-mile Aegean coastline including the port-town of Alexandroupolis' kept (the gazetteer finds both in the shape), Southern Dobruja and Kavala gone, Lozengrad, Lyule Burgas and Adrianople back with the Ottomans (Treaty of Constantinople, 30 September 1913).

correction.text: the 1913 outline plus the Ottoman land west of the Maritsa (with a 2-km strip of its eastern bank) ceded by the agreement of 6 September 1915

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe (repair pass 2026-10-25): Cliopatria's 1913 shape runs 1913-1915 and shows no change in 1915, but the page dates the Ottoman cession to 6 September 1915. Area check: 111,800 km2 (the 1913 shape) plus the page's 2,587 km2 is 114,387 km2, within 0.1 percent of the page's 114,424 km2; the gazetteer grid resolves the added land to about 1,500 km2. The land is lost again at Neuilly (November 1919).

correction.text: Cliopatria's 1916 outline (Macedonia including Skopje and Bitola, Southern Dobruja) plus the Morava lands the page says were taken in 1915 (Pirot and Zaječar 26 October, Niš 5 November, Pristina 23 November); everything beyond the 1913 frontier is occupied land, hatched, not Bulgarian territory

keyframe_review.note: 155,060 km2. The page says the lands were 'occupied' and 'captured' (Skopje 22 October 1915, Bitola 4 December 1915) and says nothing of annexation, so the ledger records them as occupation_start/_end (hatched); the outline itself fits the page for Macedonia and (per the Kingdom page) Dobruja in September 1916. Cliopatria's shape omits the Morava lands (Niš, Pirot, Zaječar, Pristina) that the page lists; the Greek part of the shape (about 4,800 km2, Eastern Macedonia) is now an occupation of 'all Greek territory east of the river Struma' (Macedonian front page; occupation_start of August 1916, ended by the armistice of September 1918).

correction.text: Cliopatria's 1917 outline unchanged, as occupied land (hatched) beyond the 1913 frontier; unverified: page budget for the Northern Dobruja part

keyframe_review.note: 171,194 km2, the largest shape. The Kingdom page says only that Bulgaria 'seized Dobruja from Romania in September 1916'. The extra 1917 land is Northern Dobruja (gazetteer: 54 cells, about 13,700 km2, 27.6-29.5 E, 43.9-45.4 N). The Treaty of Bucharest (1918) page (repair pass 2026-10-25) dates the treaty to 7 May 1918 and gives Bulgaria Southern Dobruja and only the southern part of Northern Dobruja, the rest being a Central Powers condominium, so the whole of Northern Dobruja in the 1917 and 1918 shapes is Bulgarian-held occupation, not treaty territory, and the gazetteer cannot separate the southern strip. The shape is kept as drawn as occupied land; the extent of the 1917 occupation is not on a page opened.

correction.text: Cliopatria's 1918 outline unchanged, as occupied land (hatched) beyond the 1913 frontier; unverified: page budget for the extent

keyframe_review.note: 143,738 km2. The page dates the Allied breakthrough on the Macedonian front to September 1918, Bulgaria's request for an armistice to 24 September and the armistice to 30 September 1918: the 1918 shape has lost most of Macedonia (gazetteer: about 17,700 km2 of North Macedonia and 5,600 km2 of Greek Macedonia fewer than 1917) but keeps Northern Dobruja, which the page does not date. Unverified: page budget. Repair pass 2026-10-25: Treaty of Bucharest of 7 May 1918 (never fully ratified, nullified by the armistice of 11 November 1918 and annulled by Neuilly) is now the May 1918 gain of Southern Dobruja; the Armistice of Salonica page orders the evacuation of 'Bulgarian-occupied Greek and Serbian territories' and is silent on Dobruja.

104,087 km2. The Treaty of Neuilly of 27 November 1919 took Western Thrace (Greece), 'parts of Macedonia and the Western Outlands' (Yugoslavia) and Southern Dobruja (Romania); the gazetteer finds the 1913 shape minus the 1919 shape to be about 5,300 km2 in Greece plus about 2,300 km2 of Macedonia and the Serbian border, and Northern Dobruja is gone. The shape drops them in 1919, a few weeks before the treaty date.

101,646 km2 for 1920-1923, 2,500 km2 below the 1919 shape along the southern border (gazetteer: 10 cells, 24.0-26.5 E, 41.3-41.7 N) for which no page gives a reason (the Treaty of Neuilly page mentions 'a further area of 2,563 km2 on its western border', the same size as the drop but on the western border, not the southern one where the gazetteer finds it, so it is not taken as the cause); kept as the post-Neuilly Bulgaria. No infobox area.

101,694 km2 for 1924-1940, identical in cells to 1920. The Kingdom page records coups in 1923 and 1934 and Boris III's counter-coup of April 1935 but no border change. The shape ends in 1940, but Southern Dobruja returned on 7 September 1940: see the new 1940 keyframe, which overrides the last year of this one.

correction.text: the interwar outline plus Southern Dobruja, recovered by Bulgaria in the Axis-sponsored Treaty of Craiova of 7 September 1940

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria adds Southern Dobruja (about 7,300 km2 in the gazetteer) only in its 1941 shape, a year after the treaty the page dates to 7 September 1940.

correction.text: Cliopatria's 1941 outline (Southern Dobruja kept; plus all of Greek Thrace and most of Macedonia and 'Macedonia with Pirot' after Yugoslavia and Greece were defeated) unchanged, with everything beyond the 1940 frontier as occupied land, hatched

keyframe_review.note: 153,818 km2 for 1941-1943. The page says Bulgaria 'was allowed to occupy all of Greek Thrace and most of Macedonia' and 'once again obtained a coastline to the Aegean and Macedonia with Pirot'; it says occupy, not annex, hence the hatched status in the ledger. The gazetteer finds the added land to be about 11,400 km2 in Greece, 20,500 km2 in North Macedonia and 6,300 km2 in Serbia (Pirot area). No infobox area for the war years; the page gives no year or month for the occupation.

161,314 km2, unverified: page budget. Adds about 6,800 km2 to the 1941 shape in western North Macedonia and Greek Macedonia (gazetteer: 22.98-23.73 E, 40.3-41.1 N in Greece; 20.6-20.8 E in North Macedonia), which no page opened explains: the Bulgaria in World War II page describes no 1943 extension into Greek Central Macedonia or western Macedonia (only 'In July 1943, the Bulgarian occupation zone expanded northwards' in Yugoslavia), so the 1943 occupation_start events are confidence 1. The page says only 'In August 1944 Bulgaria unilaterally announced its withdrawal from the war', gives the Soviet declaration of war as 8 September and the coup as 9 September 1944 (the World War II page: Soviet forces crossed on 8 September, the coup came 'on the eve of 8 September', the Fatherland Front government on 9 September, the armistice on 28 October 1944). Cliopatria has no Bulgarian shape for 1945-1946.

correction.text: Bulgaria allowed 'to keep Southern Dobruja' but having 'formally renounced all claims to Greek and Yugoslav territory': the interwar outline plus Southern Dobruja

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria has no Bulgarian shape between its 1944 shape and the 'Kingdom of Bulgaria' shape of 1947 (110,018 km2). The page does not date the peace settlement; the interwar outline (101,694 km2) plus Southern Dobruja (about 7,300 km2 in the gazetteer) comes within 1 percent of the 1947 area. The monarchy was abolished on 15 September 1946.

region.text: the principality 'between the Danube and the Stara Planina range, including Sofia'

ledger.note: 1878: the Treaty of Berlin creates the Principality of Bulgaria, an Ottoman vassal. 'The Principality of Bulgaria was established by the Treaty of Berlin in 1878' (13 July 1878): a 'smaller principality between the Danube and the Stara Planina range, including Sofia', while Eastern Rumelia becomes an autonomous Ottoman province and Macedonia goes back to the Sultan. Alexander of Battenberg reigns from 29 April 1879 and the Tarnovo Constitution dates from 28 April 1879.

region.text: the Principality 'subject to Ottoman suzerainty'

ledger.note: 1878: the principality is created as an Ottoman tributary state. Kingdom page: 'the establishment of the Principality of Bulgaria (subject to Ottoman suzerainty) in 1878' and 'Bulgaria had only acknowledged the overlordship of the sultan formally'; the Principality page calls it 'a vassal state under the suzerainty of the Ottoman Empire' and 'a legal fiction'. Month is the Treaty of Berlin's (13 July 1878). Mirrors the ottoman-empire vassal_start for principality-of-bulgaria (1878-7). Added in the repair pass of 2026-10-25 (reviewer eu-18-h).

region.text: Eastern Rumelia, the autonomous Ottoman province between the Balkan Mountains and the Rila and Rhodope Mountains

ledger.note: 1885: Bulgaria and Eastern Rumelia unite. 'a coup on 18 September [O.S. 6 September] 1885 supported by the Bulgarian Prince' at Plovdiv; the Tophane Agreement of 5 April 1886 recognised 'the Prince of Bulgaria as Governor-General of the autonomous Ottoman Province Eastern Rumelia', giving the union de jure recognition. Eastern Rumelia stayed an Ottoman province under the prince inside the same Ottoman relation (vassal_start of July 1878 to vassal_end of October 1908): the Tophane Agreement made the Prince of Bulgaria its Governor-General, so the union is de facto in 1885 and de jure, still under the sultan's suzerainty, from 1886.

region.text: Pirot, the Serbian ground the page says was returned in 1886, and Slivnitsa, the battle the page calls 'decisive'

ledger.note: 1885: Serbia attacks Bulgaria over the union. 'Serbia declared war on Bulgaria on 14 November' 1885 and 'suffered a quick defeat' (the page names 'the decisive Battle of Slivnitsa' but gives it no date or place; the zone therefore also takes a 30-km circle round Slivnitsa, inside Bulgaria, because the fighting was mainly in Bulgaria; the Bulgarians then 'advanced into Serbian territory up to Pirot'); the Principality page says 'Pirot and Vranya were returned to Serbia under the Treaty of Bucharest in 1886', implying Bulgarian forces held them. The page gives the declaration, not the first battle, so the month is the declaration's.

region.text: Pirot, the Serbian-Bulgarian frontier and the Slivnitsa battlefield

ledger.note: 1886: the Treaty of Bucharest ends the Serbo-Bulgarian War with no change of border. 'no changes were made along the Bulgarian-Serbian border, preserving the unification of Bulgaria' (3 March 1886); the ceasefire had been signed on 28 November 1885. The zone includes Slivnitsa, where the page puts the decisive battle (repair pass of 2026-10-25, reviewer eu-18-h).

1908: Ferdinand proclaims the independent Tsardom of Bulgaria at Veliko Tarnovo. 'On 5 October [O.S. 22 September] 1908' he declared independence and the principality was 'raised from a principality to a tsardom' (Kingdom page); same state and colour, an era caption (rule 2). The Ottoman suzerainty, 'a legal fiction' in practice, ends.

region.text: the principality with Eastern Rumelia

ledger.note: 1908: Bulgaria declares independence and the Ottoman suzerainty ends. 'On 5 October [O.S. 22 September] 1908' Ferdinand declared independence (Principality page); the Kingdom page: 'On 5 October 1908, Ferdinand declared the Independence of the Tsardom of Bulgaria'. Mirrors the ottoman-empire vassal_end for principality-of-bulgaria (1908). Added in the repair pass of 2026-10-25 (reviewer eu-18-h).

region.text: the Ottoman lands of Thrace and Eastern Macedonia that Bulgarian armies took from October 1912, until the Treaty of London

ledger.note: 1912: Bulgaria joins the First Balkan War and its armies enter Thrace and Macedonia. The page has Montenegro declaring war on 8 October 1912 and Bulgaria's war declaration delivered on '4/17 of October 1912'; Bulgaria 'attacked toward Eastern Thrace and was stopped near Constantinople at the Çatalca line', and secondary forces 'took Western Thrace and Eastern Macedonia'. The zone is the Cliopatria 1912 conquest area (1912 shape minus 1885 shape), which the page gives only in these words.

region.text: the Ottoman land west of the Enos-Midiya line 'ceded to the Balkan League', as far as Bulgaria held it: western Thrace and part of Macedonia, with Lozengrad, Lyule Burgas, Adrianople and Kavala

ledger.note: 1913: the Treaty of London cedes the Ottoman lands to the Balkan League; Bulgaria keeps western Thrace and part of Macedonia. 'The signing of the Treaty of London took place on 30 May 1913' (territory west of the Enos-Midiya line 'ceded to the Balkan League', division 'undecided'); the Treaty of Bucharest of 10 August 1913 left Bulgaria 'a portion of Macedonia, including the town of Strumnitza' and 'western Thrace with a 70-mile Aegean coastline including the port-town of Alexandroupolis'. Month is the Treaty of London's; the land is the Cliopatria 1913 gain over the 1885 shape plus (repair pass of 2026-10-25, reviewer eu-18-h) the Turkish-side and Greek-side land of the 1912 shape that the 1913 shape no longer holds: Bulgaria held it when the Treaty of London ceded it, and it is lost again at Bucharest (Kavala, August 1913) and Constantinople (Lozengrad, Lyule Burgas and Adrianople, September 1913). Without it those two losses would remove land that was never gained.

region.text: the Bregalnica front and Vardar Macedonia

ledger.note: 1913: Bulgaria attacks Serbia and Greece, opening the Second Balkan War. 'During the night of 30(17) June 1913, they attacked the Serbian army' at the Bregalnica river (attack orders dated 29 June); the Kingdom page has Bulgaria attacking Serbia and Greece on 29 June 1913. Bulgaria then lost ground in Macedonia.

region.text: Greek Macedonia from Thessaloniki and Serres to Kavala

ledger.note: 1913: Bulgaria and Greece fight over Aegean Macedonia in the Second Balkan War. The Kingdom page has Bulgaria attacking Serbia and Greece on 29 June 1913; the Balkan Wars page has 'Greece and Serbia kept the territories they had occupied'. Zone is the Greek Macedonia the Treaty of Bucharest gave Greece (Kavala and 'other Macedonian territory'), the page naming no front.

region.text: the southern part of Dobruja province

ledger.note: 1913: Romania invades Bulgaria. 'Romania had raised an army and declared war on Bulgaria on 10 July (27 June)' 1913 and met little resistance; 'Romania annexed the southern part of Dobruja province'.

region.text: Vardar Macedonia and the Bregalnica front

ledger.note: 1913: the Treaty of Bucharest ends the Second Balkan War. Signed 10 August 1913 (infobox of the Kingdom page); Greece and Serbia keep what they had occupied and Bulgaria is left Strumnitza and western Thrace.

region.text: Kavala and other Macedonian territory

ledger.note: 1913: Bulgaria gives up Kavala and Eastern Macedonia to Greece. At Bucharest (10 August 1913) 'Greece received Kavala and other Macedonian territory'; the zone is the Greek-side part of the Cliopatria 1912 shape that the 1913 shape no longer holds. The land is gained at the Treaty of London (May 1913 gain), so the loss removes land the ledger gave Bulgaria.

region.text: Greek Macedonia from Thessaloniki and Serres to Kavala

ledger.note: 1913: Bulgaria and Greece stop fighting at Bucharest. The treaty of 10 August 1913 settles Aegean Macedonia in Greece's favour.

region.text: the southern part of Dobruja province

ledger.note: 1913: Romania takes Southern Dobruja. 'Romania annexed the southern part of Dobruja province' by the Treaty of Bucharest of 10 August 1913 (also 'Romania took Southern Dobruja', Kingdom page).

region.text: the southern part of Dobruja province

ledger.note: 1913: the Dobruja war with Romania ends at Bucharest on 10 August 1913.

region.text: Lozengrad (Kirklareli), Lyule Burgas-Buni Hisar and Adrianople

ledger.note: 1913: Lozengrad, Lyule Burgas and Adrianople go back to the Ottomans. By the Treaty of Constantinople of 30 September 1913 'the regions of Lozengrad, Lyule Burgas-Buni Hisar, and Adrianople reverted to the Ottomans', the Enos-Midiya line not being accepted; the Ottomans had already won back Thrace and Adrianople in July. The land is gained at the Treaty of London (May 1913 gain), so the loss removes land the ledger gave Bulgaria.

region.text: the Ottoman lands of Thrace and Eastern Macedonia that Bulgarian armies took from October 1912

ledger.note: 1913: the Bulgarian-Ottoman contest over Thrace ends with the Treaty of Constantinople on 30 September 1913.

region.text: the remaining Ottoman lands west of the river Maritsa, including a 2-kilometer stretch on its eastern bank

ledger.note: 1915: an Ottoman-Bulgarian agreement hands Bulgaria the Ottoman land west of the Maritsa. On 6 September 1915 the agreement 'granted Bulgaria the possession of the remaining Ottoman lands west of the river Maritsa, including a 2-kilometer stretch on its eastern bank that ran along the entire length of the river', placing 'the railway to the Aegean port of Dedeagach and some 2,587 square kilometers' under Bulgarian control. Region (corrected in the repair pass of 2026-10-25, reviewer eu-18-h; the first version drew the east bank, which stayed Ottoman): the land within 20 km of the Maritsa on its west (today Greece), less the 1913 Bulgarian shape, since Dedeagach was Bulgarian already, plus the 2-km strip on the Turkish east bank. The gazetteer grid (about 250 km2 a cell) gives about 1,500 km2 against the page's 2,587 km2. Cliopatria shows no change in 1915: see the new 1915 keyframe.

region.text: Skopje, Bitola, Ohrid, Niš, Pirot, Zaječar and Pristina

ledger.note: 1915: Bulgaria enters the war and its armies occupy Serbian Macedonia and the Morava. Bulgaria declared war on Serbia on 14 October 1915; Skopje fell on 22 October, 'Pirot and Zaječar were occupied on 26 October 1915', Niš on 5 November, Pristina on 23 November, Bitola on 4 December, Debar, Struga and Ohrid within days of 29 November. The page says occupied/captured, never annexed.

region.text: 'all Greek territory east of the river Struma': Greek Eastern Macedonia

ledger.note: 1916: Bulgarian troops advance into Greek Eastern Macedonia. Macedonian front page: 'The unopposed Bulgarian advance into Greek-held eastern Macedonia precipitated a crisis in Greece' (the offensive began on 17 August 1916) and the Bulgarians 'easily conquered all Greek territory east of the river Struma'; the Greek troops were told to retreat to Kavala and 'most of the troops, including their commander, surrendered to a token German force'. The page names no town and gives no area: the region is Cliopatria's 1916 shape beyond the 1913 frontier in Greece (about 4,800 km2); 17 August is the offensive's date, not the first Greek town taken. Occupation, not annexation: the page never says annexed. Added in the repair pass of 2026-10-25 (reviewer eu-18-h).

region.text: Dobruja, seized from Romania in September 1916

ledger.note: 1916: Bulgaria seizes Dobruja from Romania. Bulgaria 'seized Dobruja from Romania in September 1916'; the page says Dobruja, not Southern or Northern, and Cliopatria draws the Southern part in 1916 and the Northern part (about 13,700 km2) from 1917.

region.text: Southern Dobruja (the Cadrilater), returned by Romania, and the southern part of Northern Dobruja

ledger.note: 1918: the Treaty of Bucharest gives Bulgaria Southern Dobruja and the south of Northern Dobruja. Signed 7 May 1918 (O.S. 24 April) at the Cotroceni Palace: 'Romania returned Southern Dobruja (the Cadrilater)' and ceded the southern part of Northern Dobruja to Bulgaria; the rest of Northern Dobruja, from the Cernavoda-Constanta railroad to the Danube, became a Central Powers condominium (a Berlin protocol of 24 September 1918 would have passed it to Bulgaria; Bulgaria capitulated five days later). King Ferdinand of Romania never signed it, the Marghiloman government denounced it in October 1918, the armistice of 11 November 1918 nullified it and the Treaty of Neuilly annulled the transfer to Bulgaria (see the Neuilly loss of November 1919). Region: Southern Dobruja only; the southern strip of Northern Dobruja is not drawn separately (Cliopatria's 1917 and 1918 shapes hold all of Northern Dobruja as occupied land). Counterpart is Romania, under the slug used for 1913 and 1916. Confidence 2: the date and the land are the page's, the region is partial. Added in the repair pass of 2026-10-25 (reviewer eu-18-h).

region.text: the Macedonian and Morava lands occupied since October 1915

ledger.note: 1918: Bulgaria asks for an armistice and gives up the occupied Serbian lands. 'The Vardar Offensive began in September 1918'; Bulgaria requested an armistice on 24 September and the armistice took effect on 30 September 1918. The page does not cover the withdrawal; the end date is the armistice's. The Armistice of Salonica page confirms that it 'ordered the evacuation of Bulgarian-occupied Greek and Serbian territories' (signed 29 September, in force at noon on 30 September 1918) but dates no evacuation.

region.text: the Greek territory east of the Struma occupied since August 1916

ledger.note: 1918: the armistice orders Bulgaria out of Greek territory. 'The armistice came into force at noon on 30 September 1918' (signed at 10:50 p.m. on 29 September) and 'ordered the evacuation of Bulgarian-occupied Greek and Serbian territories'; the page gives no date for the evacuation, so the end is the armistice's. Cliopatria's 1918 shape no longer holds this land. Added in the repair pass of 2026-10-25 (reviewer eu-18-h).

region.text: Dobruja

ledger.note: 1919: Bulgaria gives up Dobruja at Neuilly. Reviewer eu-18-h: confidence 1, no page opened dates the end of the occupation (the Bulgarian forces left after the armistice of 30 September 1918; a gap-filler should date it). The treaty's stipulations included 'the return of all conquered territories' (27 November 1919 per the Kingdom page); Cliopatria's shape drops Northern Dobruja in 1919. Neither page dates the end of the Dobruja occupation or the Treaty of Bucharest of 1918. Repair pass 2026-10-25: the Armistice of Salonica page is silent on Dobruja; the Treaty of Bucharest (1918) page says Romania re-entered the war on 10 November 1918, that the armistice of 11 November 1918 nullified the treaty and that the Treaty of Neuilly 'annulled the transfers' to Bulgaria, but not when Bulgarian troops left Dobruja; the end stays at Neuilly, confidence 1.

region.text: Western Thrace and the Aegean coast, with the Maritsa land taken in 1915

ledger.note: 1919: the Treaty of Neuilly takes Western Thrace and the Aegean coast from Bulgaria. On 27 November 1919 Bulgaria 'lost Western Thrace to Greece' and 'lost its Aegean coastline' (Kingdom page); the Neuilly page says Western Thrace went to the Entente, which gave it to Greece, and the World War I page that the treaty stipulated 'the return of all conquered territories'. Region: the Greek-side part of the Cliopatria 1913 shape that the 1919 shape no longer holds, plus (repair pass of 2026-10-25, reviewer eu-18-h) the Maritsa land gained in 1915, which lies in Thrace west of the river; that second part is my reading (no page opened says who received it in 1919), hence confidence 2. The 2-km strip on the Turkish bank goes back to the Ottomans in a separate event.

region.text: the 2-kilometer stretch on the eastern bank of the Maritsa

ledger.note: 1919: the strip on the east bank of the Maritsa goes back at Neuilly. The World War I page says the treaty stipulated 'the return of all conquered territories'; it names no recipient for the strip taken in September 1915. The east bank was Ottoman land (it stayed Ottoman in 1913), so the counterpart is the Ottoman Empire, which still existed in 1919; whether Greece held it in 1920-1923 is on no page opened. Confidence 1: the date is the treaty's and the recipient is my reading. Added in the repair pass of 2026-10-25 (reviewer eu-18-h) so that the 1915 gain is not kept after Neuilly.

region.text: parts of Macedonia and the Western Outlands

ledger.note: 1919: the Treaty of Neuilly takes border lands from Bulgaria for Yugoslavia. Bulgaria lost 'parts of Macedonia and the Western Outlands to Yugoslavia' (27 November 1919); the page names no town (Strumnitza is the Macedonian part of the 1913 shape the 1919 shape no longer holds).

region.text: Southern Dobruja

ledger.note: 1919: Southern Dobruja is returned to Romania at Neuilly. The Kingdom page lists 'Southern Dobruja to Romania' among the Neuilly losses and the Neuilly page says Bulgaria had to return Dobruja to Romania, 'thus restoring the border set by the Treaty of Bucharest (1913)'. Bulgaria had lost the land in 1913, occupied it from September 1916 and gained it by the Treaty of Bucharest of 7 May 1918 (gain of May 1918, never fully ratified; the Treaty of Neuilly annulled it), so this loss now removes land the ledger gave Bulgaria; Cliopatria's 1919 shape no longer holds it.

region.text: Southern Dobruja

ledger.note: 1940: the Treaty of Craiova gives Southern Dobruja back to Bulgaria. 'Bulgaria succeeded in negotiating the recovery of Southern Dobruja in the Axis-sponsored Treaty of Craiova' of 7 September 1940; Cliopatria adds the land in its 1941 shape.

region.text: Western Thrace and Eastern Macedonia (the page); all of Greek Thrace and the eastern part of Greek Macedonia

ledger.note: 1941: Bulgaria occupies Greek Thrace and Eastern Macedonia. 'The Greek government surrendered on 30 April; the Bulgarian occupation began the same day' (Bulgaria in World War II page, which names Western Thrace and Eastern Macedonia); the Kingdom page: 'Bulgaria was allowed to occupy all of Greek Thrace and most of Macedonia' and obtained 'a coastline to the Aegean'. Month added in the repair pass of 2026-10-25 (reviewer eu-18-h); the region is Cliopatria's 1941 shape beyond the interwar outline.

region.text: most of Macedonia and Pirot

ledger.note: 1941: Bulgaria occupies Yugoslav Macedonia and Pirot. 'On 19 April, the Bulgarian Land Forces entered Yugoslavia' (Bulgaria in World War II page, which names Yugoslav Macedonia, Pomoravlje and Eastern Macedonia but not Pirot); the Kingdom page: 'Bulgaria once again obtained a coastline to the Aegean and Macedonia with Pirot.' Month added in the repair pass of 2026-10-25 (reviewer eu-18-h); the region is Cliopatria's 1941 shape beyond the interwar outline.

region.text: the part of Greek Central Macedonia that Cliopatria's 1944 shape holds beyond its 1941 shape

ledger.note: 1943: the Bulgarian occupation zone in Greece is enlarged (bridging a silence). The Bulgaria in World War II page does not describe an extension into Greek Central Macedonia (about 4,300 km2 in the gazetteer); the land is the part of Cliopatria's 1944 shape beyond its 1941 shape and the year is the last year of the 1941 shape (1941-1943). The matching end is the 1944 occupation_end. Added in the repair pass of 2026-10-25 (reviewer eu-18-h).

region.text: the part of western Macedonia and the Morava that Cliopatria's 1944 shape holds beyond its 1941 shape

ledger.note: 1943: the Bulgarian occupation zone in Yugoslavia is enlarged (bridging a silence). The Bulgaria in World War II page says only 'In July 1943, the Bulgarian occupation zone expanded northwards', without naming land; the region is the part of Cliopatria's 1944 shape beyond its 1941 shape (about 2,500 km2 in North Macedonia, Serbia and Kosovo) and the year is the last year of the 1941 shape. The matching end is the 1944 occupation_end. Added in the repair pass of 2026-10-25 (reviewer eu-18-h).

region.text: Greek Thrace and Macedonia occupied in 1941

ledger.note: 1944: Bulgaria leaves Greek Thrace and Macedonia. 'In August 1944 Bulgaria unilaterally announced its withdrawal from the war'; the Soviet Union declared war on 8 September and the coup of 9 September 1944 followed. The page does not date the evacuation; Cliopatria's last Bulgarian shape of that extent is 1944. Bulgaria in World War II page (repair pass 2026-10-25): Soviet forces crossed the border on 8 September, the garrison coup was 'on the eve of 8 September' and the Fatherland Front government was appointed on 9 September; 'An armistice with the Allies was signed on the 28 October 1944 in Moscow'; the page does not date the evacuation of Greece and Yugoslavia, so the year stays at confidence 1. Region narrowed in the repair pass to the 1941 zone; the land added in 1943 has its own end event below.

region.text: the part of Greek Central Macedonia occupied from 1943

ledger.note: 1944: Bulgaria leaves the Greek land it held from 1943. 'In August 1944 Bulgaria unilaterally announced its withdrawal from the war' (Kingdom page); the Bulgaria in World War II page gives 8-9 September for the coup and the Soviet crossing and 28 October 1944 for the armistice, and does not date the evacuation of Greece, so the year stays at confidence 1. Pair of the 1943 occupation_start; added in the repair pass of 2026-10-25 (reviewer eu-18-h).

region.text: Macedonia and Pirot occupied in 1941

ledger.note: 1944: Bulgaria leaves Yugoslav Macedonia and Pirot. After the August 1944 withdrawal from the war and the coup of 9 September 1944, Bulgaria 'formally renounced all claims to Greek and Yugoslav territory' (peace settlement, undated on the page). The armistice with the Allies was signed on 28 October 1944 in Moscow (Bulgaria in World War II page); the evacuation is undated there. Region narrowed in the repair pass to the 1941 zone; the land added in 1943 has its own end event below.

region.text: the part of western Macedonia and the Morava occupied from 1943

ledger.note: 1944: Bulgaria leaves the Yugoslav land it held from 1943. After the August 1944 withdrawal from the war (Kingdom page) and the coup of 8-9 September, Bulgarian troops were 'hastily withdrawn from Greece and Yugoslavia'; the evacuation is undated on the pages, so the year stays at confidence 1. Pair of the 1943 occupation_start; added in the repair pass of 2026-10-25 (reviewer eu-18-h).

region.text: Bulgaria within the post-1940 borders

ledger.note: 1946: the monarchy is abolished and Bulgaria becomes a republic. 'Monarchy abolished: 15 September 1946' (infobox), following a plebiscite; Simeon II, a child under a regency, leaves the throne. Borders as kept after the war: Southern Dobruja kept, Greek and Yugoslav claims renounced.

wars.name: Serbo-Bulgarian War
wars.outcome: Bulgarian victory at Slivnitsa; ceasefire signed on 28 November 1885 and the Treaty of Bucharest of 3 March 1886 made 'no changes ... along the Bulgarian-Serbian border, preserving the unification of Bulgaria'.
wars.note: Serbia declared war on 14 November 1885. The Principality page says Pirot and Vranya 'were returned to Serbia' in 1886, which the unification page does not repeat (it says the border was left unchanged). The page names 'the decisive Battle of Slivnitsa' without date or place, so Slivnitsa (inside Bulgaria) is a second zone (repair pass 2026-10-25, reviewer eu-18-h).

wars.name: First Balkan War

zones.text: Thrace and Eastern Macedonia taken by the Bulgarian armies

wars.outcome: The Balkan League wins; the Treaty of London of 30 May 1913 cedes the Ottoman land west of the Enos-Midiya line to the League and leaves its division undecided.
wars.note: Bulgaria's declaration is dated 4/17 October 1912; Adrianople fell only after the failed January 1913 Ottoman counterattack.

wars.name: Second Balkan War
wars.outcome: Bulgaria loses: the Treaty of Bucharest (10 August 1913) leaves it Strumnitza and western Thrace, gives Kavala to Greece and Southern Dobruja to Romania; the Treaty of Constantinople (30 September 1913) returns Lozengrad, Lyule Burgas and Adrianople to the Ottomans.
wars.note: Bulgarian attack on the Serbian army at the Bregalnica on the night of 30 June 1913; Romania declared war on 10 July.

wars.name: Bulgaria in World War I
wars.outcome: Bulgaria joins the Central Powers (alliance 6 September 1915, war on Serbia 14 October 1915), takes Serbian Macedonia and the Morava in 1915 and Dobruja in September 1916, and asks for an armistice after the Vardar Offensive (effective 30 September 1918); the Treaty of Neuilly (27 November 1919) takes Western Thrace, border lands and Southern Dobruja.
wars.note: Greece's part and the Romanian front of 1916-1918 are not covered by the pages opened (page budget).

wars.name: Bulgaria in the Axis occupation of Yugoslavia and Greece
wars.outcome: 'When Yugoslavia and Greece were defeated, Bulgaria was allowed to occupy all of Greek Thrace and most of Macedonia'; Bulgaria left the war in August 1944 (Soviet declaration of war 8 September, coup 9 September 1944) and renounced all claims.
wars.note: The page gives no date or campaign for the occupation; Bulgaria did not fight Yugoslavia or Greece itself. Southern Dobruja was recovered separately, by the Treaty of Craiova of 7 September 1940.

certainty.note: Frontiers fixed by the Treaty of Berlin (1878) and, after the union of 1885, by the 3 March 1886 Treaty of Bucharest with Serbia; the Danube and the Black Sea are natural lines.
Front lines of the First Balkan War; the conquests were contested until the Treaty of London.
The treaties of Bucharest (10 August 1913) and Constantinople (30 September 1913).
Military occupation lines in Macedonia, the Morava and Dobruja.
Axis-sponsored occupation zones in Thrace, Macedonia and Pirot; Southern Dobruja is sharp (Treaty of Craiova, 7 September 1940).
Pre-1941 borders plus Southern Dobruja; the peace settlement is undated on the page.

notes: Cliopatria rows and states. (1) This row 'Principality of Bulgaria' 1880-1944 is the whole Bulgarian state: the principality of 1878-1908 and, after the independence of 5 October 1908, the Tsardom/Kingdom of Bulgaria (a rename event; the name stays the Cliopatria one). Cliopatria's Wikidata ids differ (Q815731 principality, Q147909 Kingdom of Bulgaria, Q121932 People's and Republic of Bulgaria), so the rows are not merged here, but the three describe one state; the 'Kingdom of Bulgaria' 1947 row (110,018 km2) is the same state in its last monarchical year plus one, and the dossier of the People's Republic should start at the abolition of the monarchy (15 September 1946). Cliopatria has no Bulgarian shape at all for 1945-1946: filled here by the new 1945 keyframe (interwar outline plus Southern Dobruja). (2) Statuses: the lands taken in 1915-1916 (Macedonia, the Morava, Dobruja) and in 1941 (Greek Thrace and Macedonia, Yugoslav Macedonia, Pirot) are 'occupied' on the pages, never annexed, so they are ledger occupation events, not gains, and the 1916-1918 and 1941 keyframes are adjust verdicts of status with the outline unchanged. The 1912 conquests are contested (not owned) until the Treaty of London; the 1912 shape also contains Edirne, which fell after January 1913. (3) Unverified for page budget (5 pages): the extent of the 1917 and 1918 shapes (Northern Dobruja, the Treaty of Bucharest of 7 May 1918 are on no page opened), Eastern Macedonia in 1916 (Drama, Serres, Kavala), the 1943 enlargement shown in the 1944 shape (about 6,800 km2 in western Macedonia and Greek Macedonia), and the unexplained 2,500 km2 drop from 1919 to 1920. 'Tsardom of Bulgaria' is a disambiguation page (opened, not used). (4) Disagreements: the Principality page puts the unification on 6 September 1885 (Old Style) and the unification page on 18 September [6 September O.S.]; the ledger uses September. The Principality page says Pirot and Vranya were 'returned to Serbia' in 1886, the unification page that no border changed. The Kingdom infobox gives 122,134 km2 for 1915 and the World War I page 114,424 km2 (about September 1915, plus 2,587 km2 from the 6 September 1915 Ottoman agreement); the Cliopatria 1913-1915 shape is 111,800 km2. The Balkan Wars page does not have the 26 March 1913 fall of Adrianople. (5) Names for the gazetteer: Eastern Rumelia, Western Thrace and Southern Dobruja are used only through Cliopatria-shape differences and Dobruja intersect Bulgaria; real region entries would be cleaner. Native names are not on the pages opened; they are the standard Bulgarian names. (6) Counterparts needing dossiers: Eastern Rumelia (1878-1885, autonomous Ottoman province; Cliopatria has no row; slug eastern-rumelia). Counterpart slugs used from the seed neighbours: serbs (Serbia 1885-1915), first-hellenic-republic (Greece), united-principalities-of-moldavia-and-wallachia (Romania to 1916), kingdom-of-romania, yugoslavia, ottoman-empire, people-s-republic-of-bulgaria.
